notes.text: Behold — This is the beginning of a new prophecy, which is continued from hence to the end of the next chapter. My servant - That it is Christ who is here spoken of, is so evident, that the Chaldee paraphrast, and other ancient, and some later Hebrew doctors, understand it directly of him, and that divers Jews have been convinced and converted to the Christian faith, by the evidence of this prophecy. Prosper - This is fitly put in the first place to prevent those scandals which otherwise might arise from the succeeding passages, which describe his state of humiliation. Very high - Here are three words signifying the same thing to express the height and glory of his exaltation.

Astonished — At his humiliation. Thee - At thee, O my servant. His form - Christ, in respect of his birth, breeding, and manner of life, was most obscure and contemptible. His countenance also was so marred with frequent watchings, and fastings, and troubles, that he was thought to be near fifty years old when he was but about thirty, John viii, 57, and was farther spoiled with buffetings, and crowning with thorns, and other cruel and despiteful usages.

So — His exaltation shall be answerable to his humiliation. Sprinkle - With his word or doctrine; which being often compared to rain or water, may be said to be sprinkled, as it is said to be dropped, Deut. xxxii, 2 Ezek xx, 46. Kings - Shall be silent before him out of profound humility, reverence, and admiration of his wisdom. For - They shall hear from his mouth many excellent doctrines, which will be new and strange to them. And particularly that comfortable doctrine of the salvation of the Gentiles, which was not only new to them, but strange and incredible to the Jews themselves. The incredulity of the Jews; the death of Christ, and the blessed effects thereof, ver. 1-10. His exaltation and glory, ver. 11, 12.

Who — Who, not only of the Gentiles, but even of the Jews, will believe the truth of what I say? And this premonition was highly necessary, both to caution the Jews that they should not stumble at this stone, and to instruct the Gentiles that they should not be seduced with their example. The arm - The Messiah, called the arm or power of God, because the almighty power of God was seated in him. Revealed - Inwardly and with power.

As a root — And the reason why the Jews will generally reject their Messiah, is, because he shall not come into the world with secular pomp, but he shall grow up, (or spring up, out of the ground) before him, (before the unbelieving Jews, of whom he spake ver. 1, and that in the singular number, as here, who were witnesses of his mean original; and therefore despised him) as a tender plant (small and inconsiderable) and as a root, or branch, grows out of a dry, barren ground. No form - His bodily presence shall be mean and contemptible. No beauty - This the prophet speaks in the person of the unbelieving Jews. We - Our people, the Jewish nation.
We hid — We scorned to look upon him.
Yet — Our people believed that he was thus punished by the just judgment of God.

Wounded — Which word comprehends all his pains and punishments. For our iniquities - For the guilt of their sins, which he had voluntarily taken upon himself, and for the expiation of their sins, which was hereby purchased. The chastisement - Those punishments by which our peace, our reconciliation to God, was to be purchased, were laid upon him by God's justice with his own consent. Healed - By his sufferings we are saved from our sins.

We — All mankind. Astray - From God. Have turned - In general, to the way of sin, which may well be called a man's own way, because sin is natural to us, inherent in us, born with us; and in particular, to those several paths, which several men chuse, according to their different opinions, and circumstances. Hath laid - Hebrew. hath made to meet, as all the rivers meet in the sea. The iniquity - Not properly, for he knew no sin; but the punishment of iniquity, as that word is frequently used. That which was due for all the sins of all mankind, which must needs be so heavy a load, that if he had not been God as well as man, he must have sunk under the burden.
He opened not — He neither murmured against God, nor reviled men.

Taken away — Out of this life. By distress and judgment - By oppression and violence. and a pretense of justice. His generation - His posterity. For his death shall not be unfruitful; when he is raised from the dead, he shall have a spiritual seed, a numberless multitude of those who shall believe in him. Cut off - By a violent death. And this may be added as a reason of the blessing of a numerous posterity conferred upon him, because he was willing to be cut off for the transgression of his people.

With the wicked — This was a farther degree of humiliation. He saith, he made his grave, because this was Christ's own act, and he willingly yielded up himself to death and burial. And that which follows, with the wicked, does not denote the sameness of place, as if he should be buried in the same grave with other malefactors, but the sameness of condition.

He — God was the principal cause of all his sufferings, tho' mens sins were the deserving cause. When - When thou, O God, shalt have made, thy son a sacrifice, by giving him up to death for the atonement of mens sins. His soul is here put for his life, or for himself. Shall see - He shall have a numerous issue of believers reconciled by God, and saved by his death. Prolong - He shall live and reign with God forever. The pleasure - God's gracious decree for the salvation of mankind shall be effectually carried on by his ministry and mediation.

Shall see — He shall enjoy. The travel - The blessed fruit of all his labours, and sufferings. Satisfied - He shall esteem his own and his father's glory, and the salvation of his people, an abundant recompence. By his knowledge - By the knowledge of him. Justify - Acquit them from the guilt of their sins, and all the dreadful consequences thereof. And Christ is said to justify sinners meritoriously, because he purchases and procures it for us. Many - An innumerable company of all nations. For - For he shall satisfy the justice of God, by bearing the punishment due to their sins.

I — God the father. A portion - Which is very commodiously supplied out of the next clause. With the strong - God will give him happy success in his glorious undertaking: he shall conquer all his enemies, and set up his universal and everlasting kingdom in the world. Because - Because he willingly laid down his life. Transgressors - He prayed upon earth for all sinners, and particularly for those that crucified him, and in heaven he still intercedes for them, by a legal demand of those good things which he purchased; by the sacrifice of himself, which, though past, he continually represents to his father, as if it were present. The blessings and fulness of the gospel-church, ver. 1-4. The Gentiles becoming Christ's spouse, to whom his love is everlasting, ver. 5-10. Her glories, ver. 11, 12. The gifts of the Holy Ghost, ver. 13. Her sure preservation, ver. 14-17

glossa.text: *Behold he shall understand:* lest it be doubted who said, *I who spoke, behold I am here:* and that he is the arm of the Lord, the Father plainly teaches.

*As they were astonished.* The order of the history is not kept. For above the prophet was speaking in the person of the Father concerning the Ascension of the Son, and suddenly he returned to the Passion.

*Who hath believed?* ((HIER.)) The prophet in the person of the prophets complains that few of the Jews believe what they hear from them concerning the coming of the Son.

*And the arm of the Lord.* ((ID.)) The Father announced to the world that his Son would come; and before the scandal of the cross he sent ahead the glory of him rising again. *He shall be lifted up and shall be exalted ,* etc. The choir of the prophets therefore answers that they have fulfilled their office and announced the arm of the Lord.

*A shrub.* Symmachus, a branch; signifying the man who came forth from the womb of the Virgin.

*To a thirsty one.* Aquila, *pathless,* where the privilege of virginity is shown, because without seed he was created from earth that was before pathless.
*By his bruises.* ((ID.)) It is plain that, just as his body was torn and scourged, so his soul truly grieved for us, lest in Christ part be believed truth and part falsehood.

*He opened not,* etc. To Pilate or to Herod. For he answered few things, lest the salvation of the human race be deferred.

*And as a lamb.* ((ID.)) In figure of whom the people of Israel ate the lamb in Egypt ((Exod. XII)). This is the lamb *who taketh away the sins of the world ((Joan. I))*, *who was slain from the beginning of the world ((Apoc. XIII))*, who feeds us with his flesh and his blood, and clothes us with the fleece of his protection.
*From judgment.* The judge of all found no truth of judgment, but was condemned without fault. Whence the prophet marvels that the God of all delivered himself over to the Passion.

*He shall give the wicked.* ((ID.)) That is, the Gentiles, who are without piety, to God the Father, because dead and buried he acquired them; and the rich, namely the Jews, who glory in the riches of the law and of the prophets.

*The rich.* The Scribes and Pharisees, glorying in the riches of the doctrine of the law.
*A long-lived seed.* The word of the Gospel, namely, which shall not grow old, as the Old Testament did, whence: *He that sowed went out to sow his seed ((Luc. VIII.))*

*He shall be filled.* With the faith of the Gentiles, whence, hungering and thirsting above Jacob's well, he would not use the food that had been bought, because he was already filled with the faith of the Samaritan woman and of those who were coming out to him from the city.

*And with the wicked.* That he might redeem the wicked from sin, being made all things to all: *For he bore our sins in his own body ((I Petr. II))*. Whose imitator Paul says: *I became all things to all, that I might gain all ((I Cor. IX))*.

*He prayed.* Father, forgive them. At this voice, according to the Gospel of the Nazarenes, many thousands of the Jews standing about the cross believed.

notes.text: My God — Who art my friend and father, though now thou frownest upon me. The repetition denotes, the depth of his distress, which made him cry so earnestly. Forsaken - Withdrawn the light of thy countenance, the supports and comforts of thy spirit, and filled me with the terrors of thy wrath: this was in part verified in David, but much more fully in Christ. Roaring - My out-cries forced from me, by my miseries.

But thou art — Just and true in all thy ways, this he adds to strengthen his faith, and to enforce his prayers, and prevail with God for the honour of his holy name, to hear and help him. Inhabitest - Whom thy people are perpetually praising.
A worm — Neglected and despised. People - Not only of the great men, but also of the common people. Which doth not so truly agree to David as to Christ.
Shoot out — They gape with their mouths, in mockery. This and the next verse are applied to Christ, Matt. xxvii, 39, 43.
Bulls — Wicked and violent, and potent enemies; for such are so called, Ezek xxxix, 18 Amos iv, 1. Of Bashan - As the cattle there bred were, and therefore fierce and furious.

Water — My spirits are spent and gone like water which once spilt can never be recovered; my very flesh is melted within me, and I am become as weak as water. Bones - I am as unable to help myself, and as full of torment, as if all my bones were disjointed. Wax - Melted, through fear and overwhelming grief.

Dried — I have in a manner no more moisture left in me, than is in a dry potsherd. Cleaveth - Through excessive thirst and drought. Death - Thy providence, delivering me into the power of mine enemies, and by thy terrors in my soul.

Dogs — So he calls his enemies for their insatiable greediness, and implacable fierceness against him. Pierced - These words cannot with any probability be applied to David, but were properly and literally verified in Christ.
May tell — By my being stretched out upon the cross.
They part — This also cannot be applied to David, but was literally fulfilled in Christ, Matt. xxvii, 35 John xix, 24.
Darling — Hebrew. my only one; his soul, which he so calls, because it was left alone and destitute of friends and helpers.
Heard — Answered and delivered me.

Declare — When thou hast delivered me. Thy name - that power and faithfulness and goodness, which thou hast manifested on my behalf. Congregations - The same whom he calls the congregation, and the seed of Jacob and Israel: which also does not so fitly agree to David, who never gives this title to any, but such as were near a-kin to him, as it does to Christ, who extends this name to all his disciples, Matt. xii, 48, 49, and to whom this very text is applied, Heb. ii, 11, 12.
Abhorred — He did not turn away his face from it, as men do from things which they abhor. From him - For ever: tho' he did so for a time.
Great congregation — In the universal church, of Jews and Gentiles.

Satisfied — This is doubtless to be understood, of those spiritual blessings, that grace and peace, and comfort, which all believing souls have in the sense of God's love, the pardon of their sins, and the influences of God's spirit. Seek him - That seek his favour. Your heart - He speaks of the same persons still, though there be a change from the third to the second person, as is usual in these poetical books. For ever - Your comfort shall not be short and transitory, as worldly comforts are, but everlasting.

The world — All nations from one end of the world to the other. So this is an evident prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles, and a clear proof, that this psalm immediately speaks of Christ; to whom alone, this and divers other passages of it, belong. Remember - They shall remember their former wickedness with grief and shame, and fear; particularly in worshiping dead and impotent idols. They shall remember their great and manifold obligation to God, which they had quite forgotten, his patience in sparing them so long, in the midst of all their impieties, and in giving his son for them: they shall remember the gracious words and glorious works of Christ, what he did, and suffered for them; which possibly divers of them had been eye and ear-witnesses of. The Lord - Into the only true God, and unto Jesus Christ, to whom this name of Jehovah is often ascribed in scripture.
For — This is added as a reason, why the Gentiles should be converted, because God is not only God and the Lord of the Jews, but also of the Gentiles, and of all nations.

Fat — Kings and princes, and the great men of the world. Shall eat - Shall feed upon the bread of life, Christ and all his benefits. Worship - This is added to shew what kind of eating he spoke of. Go down - That is, all mankind, for none can escape death.

A seed — Christ shall not want a seed or posterity, for though the Jewish nation will generally reject him, the Gentiles shall come in their stead. A generation - That believing seed shall be reputed both by God and men, The generation, or people of the Lord, as the Jews formerly were.

They — The seed last mentioned. Come - From Judea and Jerusalem (from whence the gospel was first to go forth) to the Gentile world, to the several parts whereof the apostles went upon this errand. His - God's righteousness: his wonderful grace and mercy unto mankind, in giving them Christ and the gospel; for righteousness is often put for mercy or kindness. Unto - Unto succeeding generations. Whereby David gives us a key to understand this psalm, and teaches us that he speaks not here of himself, but of things which were to be done in after-ages, even of the spreading of the gospel among the Gentiles, in the time of the New Testament. That he - They shall declare that this is the work of God, and not of man. David extolls the goodness of God as his shepherd, and expresses his confidence in him, ver. 1-6. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *God, my God.* ((CASS.)) A complaint of being forsaken is set before, and prayer also, as in all the psalms of the passion. ((AUG., CASS.)) *God, my God:* he doubles it out of affection, or *God* of all through the power of creation, *mine* properly through worship. ((AUG.)) When he had said this on the cross, he shewed that this psalm was written of himself. *Look upon me.* ((CASS.)) It is not in the Hebrew, but was added by the seventy interpreters. *Why hast thou forsaken me?* ((AUG.)) This is a wonder, since God also was with him; but it was for us, who in him are his body. *Far from my salvation,* that is, from that of my old man, because *salvation is far from sinners,* and these are the words not of justice, but of sins. Or, far from salvation are the words of my sins, which are to be taken away.

*I shall cry.* ((AUG.)) He speaks of us, of his own body, as when perchance he says: *Let this chalice pass from me,* that is, he is thought to have feared to die; but he said these things for his own weak ones who fear to die, and so this also is the voice of the members: *I shall cry and thou wilt not hear. By day, and thou wilt not hear, and by night, and not unto folly.* ((CASS.)) Because there are no shadows in him, and yet he is not heard unto bodily salvation.

*Thou dwellest in the holy place.* ((AUG.)) And so it is a wonder, because thou hast delivered the fathers; but I am a worm.

((CASS.)) Thou dwellest in the holy place, because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. *The praise of Israel,* ((AUG.)) that is, of him that sees thee, not of him who wished to hide himself from thy sight.
*In thee have our fathers hoped: they have hoped.* ((CASS.)) It is a great beauty, while he repeats *they have hoped.*

*But I am,* etc. ((AUG.)) Thus far Christ in the person of the old man; here now he speaks properly in his own person. *But I am.* Now properly Christ: I was born without seed, that I might be beyond men in man, in whom I was made a reproach, that at least so the pride of man might imitate the humble. *A worm and no man, a reproach.* ((CASS.)) So vilely trodden down, etc., *as far as* a worm, born without coupling, mortal, humble and vile, creeping in silence.

*He hoped in the Lord,* etc. ((CASS.)) Saying: *Hope thou in the Lord,* etc. The irony of the Jews; behold, as it were a historical narration, not a prophecy, lest there be any excuse, lest there be any ambiguity.
*From the breasts.* Not from the time when I began to be suckled, etc., *as far as* but thou hast been my God. *From the womb.*

*From the womb.* ((AUG.)) Not only of a mother, which is the law of being born for all; but from the darkness of the Synagogue, in which he is unbelieving, not yet born into the light of Christ, who trusts in those carnal observances of the sabbath and of circumcision.

*Depart not from me,* thou who hast already begun.

*Thou hast drawn me out:* not a man; lest the virgin's childbearing be doubted, it was done by the power of God. *My hope from the breasts:* true humanity and great perfection; for from the breasts he does what one scarcely come of age can do.

*In thee was I cast,* not into the sins of man. Others are cast into Adam, whence they are guilty. *From my mother's womb, my God.* ((CASS.)) Neither was the conception without God, nor in sin, as man's is; whence the Angel: *The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee.*
*They have surrounded.* ((ID.)) The passion is described, which prayer concludes; to convince the Jews he relates things to come as though they were past.

*They have opened.* ((ID.)) As wild beasts wishing to swallow him down, their mouth, not unlocked unto wisdom. *As a lion.* ((AUG.)) As a lion seizing they surrounded him, as one roaring they opened their mouth.

*As water.* When water is poured out, etc., *as far as* whence, leaving him, they fled. ((CASS.)) As water is the sacrament of the washing away of sins, etc., *as far as* and it was made solid. *Like wax.* Well does he compare the mysteries of the law to wax, etc., *as far as* for they have surrounded. *In the midst of my belly.* ((AUG.)) The belly signifies the weak in the Church, or the memory of the Church.

*My strength is dried up like a potsherd.* ((CASS.)) Not as hay, but as a potsherd, which by fire is made the firmer. *My tongue.* ((AUG.)) They kept my precepts with them, through whom I was to speak: and through them I was brought down into the kindred of those who were the dust of death.

*They have dug.* ((ID.)) The gospel narration. Although these things are so to the letter, the digging of the hands hints that they did not believe his works; of the feet, that they mangled the Apostles. ((CASS.)): they have dug. Dug earth bears fruit, so Christ wounded gave the fruit of life.

*They have numbered all my bones.* ((CASS.)) The punishment of the cross is properly described. Thus they numbered the bones, that is, the Apostles; lest they should grow into a greater number, they sought to extinguish them. *They have looked upon me.* ((ID.)) With diligence and with delight, whereas the eyes are wont to be turned away from a cruel thing. Behold how obstinate they are: nothing was done by chance, nor was their heart softened by so many miracles.

*They parted my garments among them,* etc. ((AUG.)) His own sacraments could be divided by heresies, but not the coat from above, that is, given by God; this is charity, or unity, which no man can divide. ((CASS.)) But perhaps it came to certain men even by the gift of God, etc., *as far as* as the olive branch brought by the dove to the ark. ((AUG.)) Or, through the one soul the head and the body, which being one rejects diversities.

*From the unicorns, my lowness,* etc. ((ID.)) The Jews, seeking earthly things only: or, boasting themselves singularly of the worship of God, or being singularly proud, the son also having been slain after the servants.
*Ye that fear the Lord, praise him,* etc. ((CASS.)) Human fear brings forth not praise, but blame.

*Let all the seed of Israel fear him, because he hath not despised,* etc. Whom he means by the seed of Jacob he opens, adding: *Of the poor man.* ((AUG.)) Not of him who cries out with the words of sins out of a vain life, but of him who is not swollen with the pomps of the world.
*With thee is my praise in a great church,* etc. ((ID.)) He places his praise with God, who teaches that there be no presuming in man.

*They shall praise the Lord that seek him: they shall live.* ((ID.)) The poor are rich in God: therefore poor, because they praise God that they may seek him, and he himself is the riches of the poor. *Their hearts shall remember for ever and ever, and shall be converted to the Lord.* ((ID.)) Because he is the food of the heart.

*They have eaten and have adored.* ((ID.)) Let not the dispenser forbid to eat, but let him warn the exactor to fear. *In his sight shall they fall.* ((CASS.)) The Church receives both, but he himself sees and discerns.

*It shall be shewn,* etc. ((ID.)) Or to the angels, who offer the prayers of men to God, not for instruction, but for ministry.

((CASS.)) Note that the psalms of the passion end in the great hope of Christians, that it may be known that salvation is from the passion.

notes.text: Jer. xxxi, 33, &c.

Having finished the doctrinal part of his epistle, the apostle now proceeds to exhortation deduced from what has been treated of chap. v, 4, which he begins by a brief recapitulation. Having therefore liberty to enter,

By a living way — The way of faith, whereby we live indeed. Which he hath consecrated - Prepared, dedicated, and established for us. Through the veil, that is, his flesh - As by rending the veil in the temple, the holy of holies became visible and accessible; so by wounding the body of Christ, the God of heaven was manifested, and the way to heaven opened.

Let us draw near — To God. With a true heart - In godly sincerity. Having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience - So as to condemn us no longer And our bodies washed with pure water - All our conversation spotless and holy, which is far more acceptable to God than all the legal sprinklings and washings.
The profession of our hope — The hope which we professed at our baptism.

Not forsaking the assembling ourselves — In public or private worship. As the manner of some is - Either through fear of persecution, or from a vain imagination that they were above external ordinances. But exhorting one another - To faith, love, and good works. And so much the more, as ye see the day approaching - The great day is ever in your eye.

glossa.text: *I will write over.* He does not say *I will write,* but *I will write over,* because those laws are over the strength of men, in the fulfilling of which none shall suffice, save by the help of grace. In these words it is said that he consummates by virtues, then he subjoins concerning sanctification.

*But where,* etc. Not only can it be seen from this authority that Jesus sanctifies and consummates, but also that an oblation is now, after the time of grace, not to be made for sins, when remission has been made.
*Through the veil.* Our faith is veiled, because faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof.

*In fulness of faith.* Our faith is perfect, since none of these things is now visible, neither priest nor victim. *Sprinkled in heart.* By this it is shown that not faith alone, but life with virtue is sought. *Washed with water,* that is, with baptism.
*For he is faithful.* As God is faithful in his promises, so he wills that we be faithful to him in our promises. Let us therefore have faith and confession, so far as in us lies.
*And let us consider,* etc. The perfect man by exhorting others, the lesser by imitating the perfect. Thence the Apostle exhorts to those things which befit faith.

*As the manner is.* He blames those who rend the unity of charity, as though they could not dwell among others because of their own sanctity; who rather ought by their own example to have comforted them. *But comforting.* He comforts one that labours who persists equally in the labour, because the lightening of a labour is the effort, or the striving, of him that labours with him, as happens on a journey.

notes.text: A garden — Probably belonging to one of his friends. He might retire to this private place, not only for the advantage of secret devotion, but also that the people might not be alarmed at his apprehension, nor attempt, in the first sallies of their zeal, to rescue him in a tumultuous manner. Kedron was (as the name signifies) a dark shady valley, on the east side of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives, through which a little brook ran, which took its name from it. It was this brook, which David, a type of Christ, went over with the people, weeping in his flight from Absalom. Matt. xxvi, 30; Mark xiv, 26; Luke xxii, 39.
Mark xiv, 43; Luke xxii, 47.
A troop of soldiers — A cohort of Roman foot.

As soon as he said, I am he, they went backward and fell to the ground — How amazing is it, that they should renew the assault, after so sensible an experience both of his power and mercy! But probably the priests among them might persuade themselves and their attendants, that this also was done by Beelzebub; and that it was through the providence of God, not the indulgence of Jesus, that they received no further damage.

If ye seek me, let these (my disciples) go — It was an eminent instance of his power over the spirits of men, that they so far obeyed this word, as not to seize even Peter, when he had cut off the ear of Malchus.
John xvii, 12.
Then Simon Peter — No other evangelist names him. Nor could they safely. But St. John, writing after his death, might do it without any such inconvenience.

Annas had been high priest before his son-in-law Caiaphas. And though he had for some time resigned that office, yet they paid so much regard to his age and experience, that they brought Christ to Annas first. But we do not read of any thing remarkable which passed at the house of Annas; for, which reason, his being carried thither is omitted by the other evangelists. Matt. xxvi, 57; Mark xiv, 53; Luke xxii, 54.
Art thou also — As well as the others, one of this man's disciples - She does not appear to have asked with any design to hurt him.
I spake openly — As to the manner: continually - As to the time: in the synagogue and temple - As to the place. In secret have I said nothing - No point of doctrine which I have not taught in public.
Why askest thou me — Whom thou wilt not believe?
Answerest thou the high priest so? — With so little reverence?
Now Annas had sent him to Caiaphas — As is implied ver. 13. Bound - Being still bound, ver. 12.
They went not into the palace themselves, lest they should be defiled — By going into a house which was not purged from leaven, Deut. xvi, 4. Matt. xxvii, 2; Mark xv, 1; Luke xxiii, 1.

It is not lawful for us to put any man to death — The power of inflicting capital punishment had been taken from them that very year. So the scepter was departed from Judah, and transferred to the Romans.

Signifying what death he should die — For crucifixion was not a Jewish, but a Roman punishment. So that had he not been condemned by the Roman governor, he could not have been crucified. Chap. iii, 14.

My kingdom is not of this world — Is not an external, but a spiritual kingdom; that I might not be delivered to the Jews - Which Pilate had already attempted to do, ver. 31, and afterward actually did, chap. xix, 16.

Thou sayest — The truth. To this end was I born - Speaking of his human origin: his Divine was above Pilate's comprehension. Yet it is intimated in the following words, I came into the world, that I might witness to the truth - Which was both declared to the Jews, and in the process of his passion to the princes of the Gentiles also. Everyone that is of the truth - That is, a lover of it, heareth my voice - A universal maxim. Every sincere lover of truth will hear him, so as to understand and practice what he saith.

What is truth? — Said Pilate, a courtier; perhaps meaning what signifies truth? Is that a thing worth hazarding your life for? So he left him presently, to plead with the Jews for him, looking upon him as an innocent but weak man.
Matt. xxvii, 26; Mark xv, 15.
By our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God — Which they understood in the highest sense, and therefore accounted blasphemy.
He was the more afraid — He seems to have been afraid before of shedding innocent blood.
Whence art thou? — That is, whose son art thou?

Thou couldst have no power over me — For I have done nothing to expose me to the power of any magistrate. Therefore he that delivered me to thee, namely, Caiaphas, knowing this, is more blamable than thou.

Pilate sat down on the judgment seat — Which was then without the palace, in a place called, in Greek, the pavement, on account of a beautiful piece of Mosaic work, with which the floor was adorned: but in Hebrew, Gabbatha - Or the high place, because it stood on an eminence, so that the judge sitting on his throne might be seen and heard by a considerable number of people.

It was the preparation of the passover — For this reason both the Jews and Pilate were desirous to bring the matter to a conclusion. Every Friday was called the preparation, (namely, for the Sabbath.) And as often as the passover fell on a Friday, that day was called the preparation of the passover.

Bearing his cross — Not the whole cross, (for that was too large and heavy,) but the transverse beam of it, to which his hands were afterward fastened. This they used to make the person to be executed carry. Matt. xxvii, 31; Mark xv, 20; Luke xxiii, 26.
Jesus of Nazareth, the king of the Jews — Undoubtedly these were the very words, although the other evangelists do not express them at large.

It was written in Latin — For the majesty of the Roman empire; in Hebrew - Because it was the language of the nation; and in Greek - For the information of the Hellenists, who spoke that language, and came in great numbers to the feast.
What I have written, I have written — That shall stand.
The vesture — The upper garment.

They parted my garments among them — No circumstance of David's life bore any resemblance to this, or to several other passages in the 22nd Psalm. So that in this scripture, as in some others, the prophet seems to have been thrown into a preternatural ecstasy, wherein, personating the Messiah, he spoke barely what the Spirit dictated, without any regard to himself. Psalm xxii, 18.

His mother's sister — But we do not read she had any brother. She was her father's heir, and as such transmitted the right of the kingdom of David to Jesus: Mary, the wife of Cleopas - Called likewise Alpheus, the father, as Mary was the mother of James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas.
Behold thy mother — To whom thou art now to perform the part of a son in my place, a peculiar honour which Christ conferred on him. From that hour - From the time of our Lord's death.
A stalk of hyssop — Which in those countries grows exceeding large and strong. Psalm lxix, 21.
It is finished — My suffering: the purchase of man's redemption. He delivered up his spirit - To God, Matt. xxvii, 50.

Lest the bodies should remain on the cross on the Sabbath — Which they would have accounted a profanation of any Sabbath, but of that in particular. For that Sabbath was a great day - Being not only a Sabbath, but the second day of the feast of unleavened bread (from whence they reckoned the weeks to pentecost:) and also the day for presenting and offering the sheaf of new corn: so that it was a treble solemnity.

Forthwith there came out blood and water — It was strange, seeing he was dead, that blood should come out; more strange, that water also; and most strange of all, that both should come out immediately, at one time, and yet distinctly. It was pure and true water, as well as pure and true blood. The asseveration of the beholder and testifier of it, shows both the truth and greatness of the miracle and mystery.
His testimony is true — Valid, unexceptionable. And he knoweth - And his conscience beareth him witness, that he testifieth this for no other end, than that ye may believe.
A bone of it shall not be broken — This was originally spoken of the paschal lamb, an eminent type of Christ. Exod. xii, 46.

They shall look on him whom they have pierced — He was pierced by the soldier's spear. They who have occasioned his sufferings by their sins (and who has not?) shall either look upon him in this world with penitential sorrow: or with terror, when he cometh in the clouds of heaven, Rev. i, 7. Zech. xii, 10.

Joseph of Arimathea asked Pilate — And Nicodemus also came - Acknowledging Christ, when even his chosen disciples forsook him. In that extremity Joseph was no longer afraid, Nicodemus no longer ashamed.
In the place where he was crucified — There was a garden in the same tract of land: but the cross did not stand in the garden.

Because of the preparation — That is, they chose the rather to lay him in that sepulchre which was nigh, because it was the day before the Sabbath, which also was drawing to an end, so that they had no time to carry him far.

glossa.text: *Where there was.* He is taken in a garden, that he might blot out the sin committed in the garden of delights; and into that garden, passing over the torrent of this world, he led his disciples in.

*A cohort.* Not of the Jews, but of soldiers from the governor, the order of lawful power being preserved, so that while they held him none might dare to resist; or even if any should dare, he could not prevail against so many. *He came thither.* He is betrayed by night, that he might be found without the crowds, which in the daytime were often present.
*I am he.* By this one word he who was to die laid low so many fierce and strong men, by the power of the Godhead lying hidden: because he willed indeed to be seized, but not save when he willed.

*They went backward and fell to the ground.* So now Christ says everywhere through the Gospel, I am he, and the Jews, awaiting Antichrist, go backward and fall into the earthly things which they love.

*Let these go their way. ((AUG.))* They do what he commands; they let those go whom he wills not to perish: not but that they should die afterwards, but because they did not yet believe as those believe who do not perish.

*Put up.* As if he said: Let vengeance rest. Otherwise: Turn thy sword into its own place, that is, turn the word of preaching to the Gentiles, where, according to Paul, a door open and great may be found. Otherwise, after the fulness shall have come in, he says to Peter, by whom the whole order of preachers is designated: Send the word of preaching to Israel. *For all that shall take the sword shall perish by the sword ((Matth. XXVI))*. By what sword? By that fiery one which is turned before paradise: and by the sword of the spirit, which is written of in the armour of God.
*And the cohort.* It was the custom with the Jews that whomsoever they judged worthy of death they delivered bound to the governor.

*And they led him away.* There were at that time two chief priests (as Luke says), Annas and Caiphas, who held their years by turns. But then it was the year of Caiphas, and by his will Jesus was first led to Annas, not because he was his colleague but because he was his father-in-law. Or the houses were so placed that Annas ought not to be passed by by those going by.
*And another disciple.* Who this may be, since it is here kept silent, let it not be rashly determined. Yet this John is accustomed so to signify himself.

*He saith: I am not. ((AUG.))* Not only does he deny Christ who says that he is not the Christ, but he also who denies that he is a Christian; and so is fulfilled that which the Lord said: *Thou shalt deny me thrice ((Matth. XXVI))*.

*Why askest thou me?* That is, from whom thou desirest not to hear the truth. Ask rather those of whose sayings thou mayest have no ill-will. So he tempers his answer that he neither kept the truth silent, nor seemed to be defending himself.

*And when he had said these things.* It is objected, why he did not do what he taught. He ought not to have answered thus, but to have offered the other cheek. But he answered truthfully and meekly and justly, and made ready for the smiter not his cheek only, but his whole body. And hence he rather showed that the precepts of patience are to be fulfilled not by an ostentation of the body, but by a preparation of the heart; for a man can offer his cheek visibly and be angry. Better, therefore, does he answer who is truly appeased, and with a tranquil mind ready to bear heavier things.
*If I have spoken ill.* He speaks ill who speaks against the truth. If I have spoken ill, give testimony whereby thou mayest prove me a liar.

*And there was. ((AUG.))* Having said that Annas sent Jesus to Caiphas, he returns to the place of the narrative where he had left Peter, that he may unfold what had befallen in the house of Annas concerning Peter's threefold denial.

*Into the hall.* That is, where Pilate the governor dwelt. But if to Caiphas, how into the hall? perhaps, some cause pressing, both had come together from the house of Annas to hear Jesus. Caiphas went on to the governor's hall, and left Jesus to his father-in-law to be heard; or in the house of Caiphas Pilate had taken his hall, and the house was so great that the master dwelt apart and Pilate apart. *That they might not be defiled.* Because in the days of unleavened bread it was a defilement to them to enter into the dwelling of a stranger.

*It is not lawful for us,* etc. This they say because of the holiness of the feast day. For the law commands that they spare not evildoers, especially such as seduce men from their God, which they said this man was; and they speak against themselves, because they were killing him whom they were offering up to be killed, as Pilate also killed, yet not with his own hands. When Pilate wished to deliver Jesus to the Jews, that according to their own law they might judge him, they refused to receive him, saying: *It is not lawful for us to put any man to death;* and so is fulfilled the word of Jesus which he foretold concerning his own death, that, being delivered up by the Jews, the Gentiles should kill him, as though they were thus strangers to the crime who sin the more; wherein not their innocence but their madness is shown.

*Sayest thou this of thyself,* etc. Jesus knows what he himself asks and what the other will answer, but yet he willed it to be said, not that he might know, but that what he willed to know might be written.

*What hast thou done.* As if: If this be no fault, that thou hast called thyself king, what else hast thou done? As if: it is no wonder if thou art delivered to a judge to be punished, thou who callest thyself king. But if this were not the cause, then perhaps another must be sought; as if: confirm whether this be the cause which is objected, or another.

*A kingdom.* This is what he willed us to know; but first, by asking in his turn, he willed to show what was the opinion of men concerning his kingdom, of Jews or of Gentiles; and this being shown, he answers more fitly to both: *My kingdom is not of this world.* As if: ye are deceived; for I hinder not your dominion in this world, that ye may not vainly fear and be in servitude, but to come by believing to the heavenly kingdom.

*Thou sayest.* He fears not to confess himself a king, but it is so set free that he neither denies himself a king, nor confesses himself to be of the world, as he supposed who said: *Art thou a king then?* To whom he answered: *Thou sayest that I am a king.* As if he should say, being carnal thou speakest carnally.
*Again.* He waits not for an answer, lest, when he wished to release him, there should be delay; for suddenly there came into his mind the custom whereby one might be released at the Pasch.
*But there is.* Because at the Pasch they were freed from servitude, at the Pasch this custom of releasing was theirs.

*Now Barabbas was a robber.* That is, son of a master, that is, of the devil, who was a master to the robber in his crime, to the Jews in their treachery. Or Barabbas, that is, son of the father, that is, of the devil.
*Then therefore.* This Pilate did, that is, he permitted the soldiers to do it, or even commanded it, that the Jews, being sated with the punishments, might desist from his death.

*They put on a crown of thorns.* In the crown of thorns is marked the taking up of our sins, for which he willed to become mortal. Whence the forerunner: *Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sins of the world.* For thorns are set down in the signification of sins. Whence the Lord: *Thy earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles ((Gen. III))*. That is, thy conscience shall not cease to bring forth prickings and the stings of vices.
*He went forth therefore.* Behold, there are fulfilled the things which Jesus had foretold of himself by his hidden power; his patience is commended, by which the martyrs are formed.

*And he saith to them.* Here it appears that these things were done by the soldiers not without Pilate's knowledge, whether he commanded or permitted them, that, the Jews being sated, these things might suffice; but they burn the more and cry out: *Crucify, crucify.*
*The Son of God.* Behold another and greater ill-will, because the unlawful aspiring to a kingdom seemed a small thing; and yet Christ was truly both, both king and Son of God.

*But Jesus.* Here and in other places Christ is read to have kept silence, that the prophecy might be fulfilled: *As a lamb before his shearer, without voice, so he opened not his mouth ((Isa. LIII))*. Which likeness is taken from the lamb, that in his silence he may be held not guilty but innocent. For he is not convicted as one conscious of guilt, but as a meek one he is sacrificed for others.

*And from thenceforth.* That is, from this cause, lest he should have the sin of slaying an innocent man (and if less so to those envious men), he sought to release him: not that he then first sought it, but if before he wished it, now he sought it.

*If thou release this man, thou art not a friend.* Above they set forth the law, according to which he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God: but because that man fears not the law of a foreign nation, and rather fears to slay the Son of God, they frighten him with Caesar, whom he cannot despise as the author of his own power.
*And it was the parasceve. ((AUG.))* Parasceve, which is interpreted *preparation,* etc., *down to* and the same is the sixth of the preparation.

*Shall I crucify your king?* Still he tries to overcome the terror which they press upon him concerning Caesar, saying: *Shall I crucify your king?* Wishing to break them by their own shame, whom by the shame of Christ he could not soften.

*Then therefore.* Because they openly declare that Caesar is against him if he wish to press another king upon them, by releasing unpunished the man whom on account of these presumptions they had delivered to be slain. Overcome therefore by fear, he delivered Jesus to them that he might be crucified. *He delivered Jesus to them to be crucified.* To them: not that they should themselves take him with their hands, who above had excused themselves from this, but that they may be seen implicated in the crime from which they try to be strangers, since Pilate did this for none but them; whence he does not say that they should crucify him, but that he should be crucified by the judgment and power of Pilate.

*Bearing.* Jesus was bearing his own cross. A great mockery to the impious, a great mystery to the pious who glory in it, as in the sceptre of a kingdom; and the cross is the candlestick of the lamp which was not to be placed under a bushel. First the Lord bears the cross, because he suffered first; afterwards it was laid upon Simon of Cyrene, because we ought to follow in his steps.
*And with him.* The robber who remained in unbelief signifies the Jews; he who confesses signifies the Gentiles.

*And it was written.* These three tongues were eminent above the rest: Hebrew, because of the Jews glorying in the law of God; Greek, because of the wise men of the nations; Latin, because of the Romans, who then ruled over almost all nations.

*The soldiers therefore, when they had crucified him.* Behold what things were done beside the cross, when he was now crucified.

*Four.* The fourfold garment signifies the Church spread through the whole world, which consists of four parts, distributed equally to all its parts, that is, harmoniously. The tunic assigned by lot signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of charity. *From above.* Because charity is eminent above all things throughout the whole, because no one is without it who is seen to belong to the whole; from which whole, as the Greek tongue indicates, the Church is called catholic, which in the lot is commended by the grace of God.

*When Jesus therefore had seen his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved.* He who, being about to do divine things, as it were repelled his mother as one unknown, now shows that the hour has come which he then foretold, in which he acknowledges her of whom he had been mortally born. And he teaches that care is to be bestowed by dutiful sons upon their parents; whence the Apostle also: *If any man have not care of his own, he denieth the faith ((I Tim. V))*, etc.

*And from that hour the disciple took her.* Who, although he had now nothing of his own, had received a hundredfold in that fellowship where all things were common, having nothing and possessing all things.

registers.label: Spare
lines: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
He was wounded for our transgressions.
He was despised, and we held him of no account.
Upon him was the punishment that made us whole.
From the cross he cries, It is finished.
By his wounds we are healed.
Let us draw near in silence to the cross.
We behold the Lamb of God. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: On a hill outside the wall they lift him up between two thieves, and the sky goes dark over Jerusalem.
By his wounds we are healed.
He was despised and rejected, a man of sorrows, and we hid our faces from him.
By his wounds we are healed.
He was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that made us whole fell on him.
By his wounds we are healed.
From the dry ground of the cross he cries out, My God, why have you forsaken me, and then: It is finished.
By his wounds we are healed.
So let us draw near with confidence, through the curtain of his torn flesh, and worship.
By his wounds we are healed. Amen.
